...or so I say. Ekasmim brahmacariyasmiṃ means in one Dhamma teaching. For here, the Dhamma teaching itself is intended by the term brahmacariya. Maccuhāyinaṃ refers to the Arahants who have completely abandoned death.

In this Pāḷi, dasā ca dasadhā dasā, dasā is ten (10), and dasadhā dasā is a hundred (100); thus (Sahampati Brahma) says, "I see another hundred and ten (110) learners (sekha)." Sotasamāpannā refers to those who have reached the stream of the Path. Atiracchānagāmino is merely a conventional teaching; it means those who do not have the nature of falling into the lower realms. Saṅkhātuṃ nopi sakkomi means that for fear of the danger of lying, he is unable to count or define, saying, "There are this many beings who share in merit." This is said with reference to the vastness of the Brahma's Dhamma teaching. The third (Sekha) Sutta is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Aruṇavatī Sutta
In the fourth sutta, Abhibhūsambhava refers to the Elder Abhibhū and the Elder Sambhava. Among those two, the Elder Abhibhū was foremost in wisdom like the Venerable Sāriputta, and the Elder Sambhava was foremost in concentration like the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. Ujjhāyanti means they criticize, or they think in a lowly manner. Khiyyanti means they say to one another, "What kind of matter is this?" Vipācenti means they speak repeatedly while spreading the word. Heṭṭhimena upaḍḍhakāyena means with the lower half of the body starting from the navel. Only this much appears in the Pāḷi text.

The Elder, however, showed various psychic transformations as mentioned in the method of the Paṭisambhidāmagga, such as "abandoning the natural form and taking the form of a Nāga, or taking the form of a Garuḍa." "He spoke these verses" means the Elder thought, "In what way should the Dhamma teaching be taught so that it would be dear and pleasing to all?" While reflecting thus, he knew: "All heretics and all gods and humans praise the effort of men in their own doctrines; there is no one who speaks ill of energy (vīriya). Therefore, I will teach a Dhamma connected with energy. If I teach thus, this Dhamma teaching will be dear and pleasing to all." Having searched and investigated the Three Piṭakas, he spoke these verses.

In those verses, ārambhatha means "exert the energy of inception." Nikkamatha means "exert the energy of launching." Yuñjatha means "make an effort, strive." Maccuno senaṃ means the army of Death is indeed the army of defilements; "crush and destroy that army." Jātisaṃsāraṃ means...
204:
'Jātiñca saṃsārañca' means birth and the round of rebirths, or the round of rebirths known as birth. 'Dukkhassantaṃ karissatīti' means he will make an end to the suffering of the round (vaṭṭa-dukkha). In what manner did the Elder Abhibhū make the thousandfold world-system aware? First, having attained the blue kasiṇa, he pervaded with darkness all places where there was light. Having attained the white kasiṇa, he pervaded with light the places where there was darkness. Then, when the reflection 'What is this darkness?' arose in beings, he showed them light. Since there is no need to produce light in a place already lit, he showed himself to the gods and humans who were searching and wondering, 'What is this light?' Then, saying to them, 'I am the Elder Abhibhū,' he recited these verses. Everyone heard the sound as if it were a Dhamma-preacher sitting and teaching in the midst of an assembled audience. The meaning also became clear to those gods and humans. The fourth sutta is finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Parinibbāna Sutta

In the fifth sutta, 'upavattane mallānaṃ sālavaneti': Just as one must go from the bank of the Kadamba river through the gate of the Rājamātu Vihāra to the Thūpārāma, so there is a Sal grove park on the opposite bank of the river named Hiraññavatī. Just as the Thūpārāma of Anurādhapura is in the southwest corner, so is that Sal grove in relation to the city of Kusinārā. Just as the road entering the city from the south gate of the Thūpārāma goes facing east and then turns north, so the row of Sal trees from the park goes facing east and then turns north. Therefore, that place is called 'Upavattana'. It took place in that Sal grove of the Mallas called Upavattana. 'Antarena yamakasālānanti' means in the space between the Sal trees which stood intertwined with one another by their roots, trunks, branches, and leaves. 'Appamādena sampာဒေထာတိ' means accomplish your necessary duties through a state of living not devoid of mindfulness (sati). Thus, just as a wealthy householder lying on his deathbed might tell his sons the essence of his wealth, the Blessed One, lying on the bed of his Parinibbāna, spoke by condensing all the instructions he had given for forty-five years into the single word 'heedfulness' (appamāda). 'Ayaṃ tathāgatassa pacchimā vါစာတိ' (This is the last word of the Tathāgata): these are the words of the Elders who conducted the Recitation (Saṅgītikāras). After this, in order to show how the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna after making the preparations for it, it is said: 'Then the Blessed One [entered] the first jhāna,' and so on. There, while the Blessed One had attained the cessation of perception and feeling (saññāvedayitanirodha), seeing that there was no more in-breathing and out-breathing, the gods and humans cried out all at once, thinking, 'The Teacher has attained Parinibbāna.' The Elder Ānanda also asked, 'Venerable Anuruddha, has the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna?'
205:
Elder Ānanda questioned Elder Anuruddha. Elder Anuruddha said, "Friend Ānanda, the Blessed One has not yet attained parinibbāna; rather, he is in the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling." How did Elder Anuruddha know? It is said that Elder Anuruddha followed the Teacher through each attainment, and by following him up to the emergence from the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he knew: "Now the Blessed One has reached the attainment of cessation, and there is no such thing as passing away within the attainment of cessation."

Then the Blessed One, having emerged from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, entered the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception... [pe]... emerging from the third jhāna, he entered the fourth jhāna. In this context, the Blessed One entered the first jhāna in 24 instances, the second jhāna in 13 instances, and likewise the third jhāna, and the fourth jhāna in 15 instances. How? He first entered the first jhāna in these 24 instances: the 10 foulness (asubha), the 32 parts of the body (dvattiṃsākāra), the 8 kasinas, loving-kindness (mettā), compassion (karuṇā), appreciative joy (muditā), mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna), and the space-limit (paricchedākāsa). Excluding the 32 parts of the body and the 10 foulness, he entered the second jhāna in the remaining 13 instances, and the third jhāna in those same instances. He entered the fourth jhāna in these 15 instances: the 8 kasinas, the divine abiding of equanimity (upekkhā-brahmavihāra), mindfulness of breathing, the space-limit, and the 4 immaterial states (arūpa). This is just a brief explanation. The Blessed One, the Lord of Dhamma, entering the city of Nibbāna, entered all the 2,400,000,000,000 attainments, experiencing all the bliss of the attainments before entering, just as a person going to another place embraces his relatives in farewell.

"Emerging from the fourth jhāna, immediately thereafter the Blessed One attained parinibbāna." In this context, there are two types of "immediately thereafter": "immediately after jhāna" (jhānasamanantara) and "immediately after reviewing" (paccavekkhaṇasamanantara). Attaining parinibbāna in the life-continuum (bhavanga) immediately after emerging from the fourth jhāna is called "immediately after jhāna." Attaining parinibbāna in the life-continuum after emerging from the fourth jhāna and then reviewing the jhāna factors is called "immediately after reviewing." Both of these are "immediately thereafter." The Blessed One, having entered jhāna, emerged from it, reviewed the jhāna factors, and then attained parinibbāna with the life-continuum consciousness (bhavanga-citta), which is indeterminate (abyākata) and included in the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca). Indeed, all beings, from Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Noble Disciples down to the smallest red or black ants, pass away only with the life-continuum consciousness, which is indeterminate and included in the truth of suffering.
206:
'Bhūtā' means beings. 'Appaṭipuggalo' means he is a person without an equal. 'Balappatto' means he has reached the ten powers of knowledge. 'Uppādawayadhammino' means having the nature of arising and passing away. 'Tesaṃ vūpasamo' means the stilling of those formations (which is the unconditioned state). 'Sukho' means the meaning is that Nibbāna itself, which is not conditioned by causes, is happiness. The word 'tadāsī' was spoken by Elder Ānanda in reference to the earthquake described in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta: "Simultaneously with the Parinibbāna, there was a great earthquake." That earthquake was both hair-raising and terrifying. 'Sabbākārawarူpete' means the Blessed One who is endowed with excellent qualities in every way. 'Nāhu assāsapassāso' means inhalation and exhalation occurred no more. 'Anejo' means the Buddha who is free from passion because of the absence of the 'agitation' (ejā) known as craving. 'Santimārabbha' means referring to, depending on, or in view of the Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbāna). 'Cakkhumā' means the Great Buddha who has vision through the five eyes. 'Parinibbuto' means he attained Parinibbāna through the Parinibbāna of the aggregates (khandha-parinibbāna). 'Asallīnena' means with a mind that is unattached and well-radiant. 'Vedanaṃ ajjhāwasayī' means he endured the painful feeling; he did not follow the feeling, nor did he toss and turn to and fro. 'Vimokkho' means liberation, which is unobstructed by any state, having reached the state of being beyond designation in every way, became like the extinguishing of a lamp. This is the fifth sutta.

## The Second Chapter (Vagga).

## Thus, in the Sāratthappakāsinī, the Commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya,

## The Commentary on the Brāhmaṇa Saṃyutta is concluded.
207:
## 7. Brāhmaṇasaṃyutta
## 1. Arahantavagga

In the first sutta of the Brāhmaṇasaṃyutta, 'Dhanañjānī' is so called because she belongs to the Dhanañjāni lineage. That brahmin woman was of noble birth, it is said. The other brahmins believe that they are born from the mouth of Brahma, while those of the Dhanañjāni lineage came forth by splitting the head; such is their view. Regarding the phrase 'uttered an inspired utterance' (udānaṃ udānesi), why did she utter it? That brahmin [her husband] was a person of wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi); when the words 'Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha' were spoken, he would plug his ears; he was as stubborn as a khadira stump. The brahmin woman, however, was a noble disciple, a stream-enterer (sotāpanna). When the brahmin gave alms, he would give thick milk-rice unmixed with water to five hundred brahmins; the brahmin woman would offer food of various flavors to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. On the day of the brahmin's feast, the brahmin woman, out of obedience to her husband and because she had abandoned stinginess (macchariya), would serve with her own hands. But on the day of the brahmin woman's offering, the brahmin would leave the house early in the morning and run away.

Then one day, the brahmin, without consulting the brahmin woman, invited five hundred brahmins and said to her, 'Lady, tomorrow five hundred brahmins will eat in our house.' She asked, 'O Brahmin, what must I do?' He replied, 'Lady, there is nothing else for you to do; others will handle all the cooking and serving. However, whether you are standing, sitting, sneezing, or coughing, you usually perform the salutation "Namo Buddhassa" (Homage to the Buddha) to that shaven-headed wretched ascetic; do not do that for just this one day tomorrow. Upon hearing those words, the brahmins will become displeased; do not cause a rift between me and the brahmins.' She replied, 'Whether you are separated from the brahmins or from the devas, I, recollecting the Teacher, cannot remain without paying homage.' He said, 'Lady, in a village of well-bred men, they even strive to close the village gate; can you not close your mouth, which can be closed with just two fingers, for the duration of the brahmins' meal?' Although he spoke thus repeatedly, he was unable to stop her. Therefore, taking up a disk-tipped sword that was placed at the head of the bed, he said, 'Lady, if tomorrow while the brahmins are sitting...'
208: "...you pay homage to that shaven-headed wretched ascetic, I will mince you with this sword from the soles of your feet to the tips of your hair like a tender bamboo shoot and make a heap of you," and he spoke this verse: "With this curved sword, from feet to head, I will cut you like a tender bamboo shoot, if you do not follow my wish. If you say 'Buddha', if you speak 'Dhamma', if you praise 'Saṅgha', while living in my house (I will cut you)." But noble disciples are difficult to shake like the great earth, and difficult to turn back like Sineru, the king of mountains. That Dhanañjānī brahmin woman replied to her husband thus: "Brahmin, if you wish, cut my limbs great and small as you please; I will never depart from the teaching of the Excellent Buddha. I am not one who bears her final body yet, so I cannot be stopped from words concerning the Buddha's grace; I am a daughter of the Excellent Buddha; cut me or kill me as you wish." Thus, roaring the so-called "Dhanañjānī's roar," she spoke five hundred verses. The brahmin, unable to touch or strike the brahmin woman, said, "Lady, do as you please," and threw the sword onto the bed. The next day, he had the house smeared with fresh cow dung, decorated here and there with parched rice, full jars, flowers, scents, and so on, and had milk-rice with little water prepared with fresh ghee, sugar, and honey for the five hundred brahmins, and announced the time. The brahmin woman also bathed herself with scented water early in the morning, put on a new cloth worth a thousand (pieces), placed another cloth worth five hundred over one shoulder, and being adorned with all ornaments, she took a golden ladle and served the brahmins in the dining hall. While she was offering milk-rice to that brahmin who was sitting in the same row with those brahmins, she slipped on a piece of wood that was poorly placed. Due to the impact of the slip, painful feeling arose. At that moment, she recollected the One of Ten Powers. Being endowed with mindfulness, she did not drop the bowl of milk-rice but lowered it gently, placed it well on the ground, and in the midst of the five hundred brahmins, she placed her hands in anjali on her head, bowed towards the direction of the Veḷuvana monastery, and uttered this inspired utterance: "Namo Tassa..."
209:
At that time, among those five hundred Brahmins, some had finished eating, some were still eating, some had just lowered their hands, and for some, the food had just been placed before them. Upon hearing that sound (of "Namo Tassa"), they experienced suffering and displeasure, as if they had been struck on the head with a mallet the size of Mount Sineru, or as if a spike had been driven into their ears. Getting angry, they said, "This woman of another faith has brought us into this house!" They threw away the morsels of food in their hands, spat out the food in their mouths, and, like crows seeing a bow, they fled in all directions while reviling the Brahmin.

Seeing the Brahmins departing in such disarray, the Brahmin looked at the Brahmin woman from head to toe and reviled her in various ways, saying, "You wretch! Foreseeing this very danger, I have been pleading with you since yesterday, but to no avail." He then said words such as, "This is how it has turned out."

Regarding "Upasaṅkami" (He approached): He thought, "The ascetic Gotama is one honored by villages, market towns, and kingdoms. It is not possible to go and threaten him by saying just anything. I will ask him only one question." While on his way, he composed the verse beginning with "Kiṃsu chetvā" (Having cut what...), thinking: "If he says, 'I approve of the killing of such and such a person,' then I will refute him by saying, 'You wish to kill those whom you do not like; you have arisen for the destruction of the world. What is the use of your state as an ascetic?' If he says, 'I do not approve of the killing of anyone,' then I will refute him by saying, 'So you do not even desire the destruction of lust and so forth? Why then do you wander about as an ascetic?' Thus, the ascetic Gotama will be able neither to swallow nor to spit out this double-edged question." Thinking thus, he approached. "Sammodi" (He exchanged greetings) means that due to his own wisdom, he did not show his anger but spoke sweet words and greeted him joyfully. That question was spoken in the Devatā Saṃyutta. The remaining words are just as explained in detail below. The first sutta is finished.

## 2. Akkosasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, "Akkosaka Bhāradvāja" refers to that same Bhāradvāja, but because he came reviling the Blessed One with about five hundred verses, the redactors of the Council gave him the name "Akkosaka Bhāradvāja." "Kupito anattamano" (Angry and displeased) means that he was angry with wrath and had a dissatisfied mind due to sorrow, thinking, "By ordaining my elder brother, the ascetic Gotama..."
210:
"...has caused the loss of our kinsmen; the faction has been broken." This is the meaning. "Akkosati" (He reviles) means he reviles with the ten grounds for abuse: "You are a thief, you are a fool, you are a deluded one, you are a robber, you are a camel, you are a goat, you are an ox, you are a donkey, you are an animal, you are a denizen of hell." "Paribhāsati" (He threatens) refers to saying such things as, "Wait, you shaveling petty ascetic! Do you think, 'I am beyond punishment'? Now I will take you to the royal palace and have you punished."

Eating together is called "Sambhuñjati." Retaliating against one who reviles is called "Vītiharati." Why did he say "Venerable Gotama" in this way? It is said that upon hearing the words, "Brahmin, this belongs only to you; Brahmin, this belongs only to you," he thought, "It is heard that when ascetics get angry, they curse like the ascetic Kisavaccha and others." Based on this hearsay, the fear arose in him, "I think the ascetic Gotama is cursing me." Therefore, he spoke thus.

One who is free from the agitation of defilements is called "Danta" (Tamed). One who has reached the characteristic of "suchness" (equanimity) is called "Tādi." Evil comes to that person who retaliates with anger because of that very anger. Being endowed with mindfulness and enduring is called "Sato upasammati" (Calms down with mindfulness). Practicing for the benefit of both oneself and others, and healing the disease of defilements, is called "Ubhinnaṃ tikicchantaṃ." It is exactly as in this Pali text. A person who is mindful and calm, who practices for the benefit of both, who heals, and who accomplishes this—blind foolish worldlings who are unskilled in the Dhamma regard that person as a "fool." "Dhamma" here refers to the Dhamma of the five aggregates or the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. The second sutta is finished.

## 3. Asurindakasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, Asurindaka Bhāradvāja is the younger brother of Akkosaka Bhāradvāja. He was angry for that same reason (his brother's ordination). That victory belongs only to the one who endures. To whom does that victory belong? This victory belongs only to the one who knows the benefit of endurance.
211:
The fool, who does not know the benefit of patience (forbearance), speaks harsh words and thinks, "I am the winner," believing he has truly won. The commentary on the third sutta (Asurindaka Sutta) ends.

## 4. Bilangīkasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fourth sutta, "Bilangīka Bhāradvāja" refers to a man whose original name was simply Bhāradvāja. However, because he prepared and sold various types of fermented gruel (kañjika), both pure and mixed with ingredients, and accumulated much wealth, the Recorders of the Council gave him the name "Bilangīka Bhāradvāja." "Tuṇhībhūto" means he stood in silence, unable to say a single word because he was extremely angry, thinking, "This ascetic Gotama has made my three elder brothers go forth (into monkhood)." The verse spoken by the Buddha has already been explained in the Devatā Saṃyutta. The commentary on the fourth sutta ends.

## 5. Ahimsakasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fifth sutta, "Ahimsaka Bhāradvāja" refers to this Bhāradvāja who was given this name by the Recorders of the Council because he used to ask questions about non-violence (ahimsā). Alternatively, he was Ahimsaka by name and Bhāradvāja by clan. "Ahimsakāhaṃ" means he addressed the Buddha saying, "May the Venerable Gotama know me as one named Ahimsaka." "Tathā cassa" means, "Brahmin, if your name is indeed Ahimsaka, may you be a person who fulfills the meaning of that name." "Na hiṃsati" means he does not harm or cause suffering. The commentary on the fifth sutta ends.

## 6. Jaṭāsutta-vaṇṇanā

In the sixth sutta, "Jaṭā Bhāradvāja" refers to this Bhāradvāja who was called so by the Recorders of the Council because he asked the question about the "tangle" (jaṭā). The remaining words have already been explained in the Devatā Saṃyutta. The commentary on the sixth sutta ends.

## 7. Suddhikasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, "Suddhika Bhāradvāja" refers to this Bhāradvāja who was called so by the Recorders of the Council because he asked the question about "purity" (suddhi). "Sīlavāpi tapokaraṃ" means even if one is endowed with virtue or performs ascetic practices (tapokamma). In the phrase "Vijjācaraṇasampanno," "Vijjā" refers to the Three Vedas. "Caraṇa" refers to the conduct of the lineage (gottacaraṇa). "So sujjhati na aññā itarā pajā" means only that Brahmin who is proficient in the Three Vedas is pure, whereas this other...
212:
...other ignorant beings are not pure. "Bahumpi palapaṃ jappaṃ" means reciting many words, saying "Only the Brahmin is pure," thus speaking thousands of such words. "Antokasambu" means one who is rotten within because of the nature of the putridity of defilements. "Saṅkiliṭṭho" means one who is endowed with defiled bodily actions and so forth. The commentary on the seventh sutta ends.

## 8. Aggikasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the eighth sutta, "Aggika Bhāradvāja" refers to this Bhāradvāja who was given this name by the Recorders of the Council due to his practice of tending the fire (fire-worship). "Sannihito hoti" means it is prepared with ghee. "Aṭṭhāsi"—why did he stand there? It is said that when the Blessed One surveyed the world at dawn, he saw this Brahmin and thought: "This Brahmin, taking such excellent milk-rice (pāyāsa) and thinking 'I will feed the Great Brahmā,' is making it fruitless by burning it in the fire; he is descending onto the path to the states of deprivation (apāya). If he does not give up this view, he will surely fill the states of deprivation. I shall go and preach the Dhamma to him, destroy his wrong view, ordain him, and give him the four paths and the four fruits." Therefore, he entered Rājagaha in the morning and stood at that Brahmin's house.

"Tīhi vijjāhi" means by the Three Vedas. "Jātimā" means being endowed with a pure lineage for seven generations back to the grandfathers. "Sutavā bahū" means one who has heard many various texts. "Somaṃ bhuñjeyya" means that Brahmin proficient in the Three Vedas is fit to eat this milk-rice, but for you, this milk-rice is not fit.

"Vedī" means he knew and penetrated with the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa). "Saggāpāyaṃ" means he sees both heaven and the states of deprivation with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). "Jātikkhayaṃ" means the fruit of Arahatship. "Abhiññāvosito" means having known the Four Noble Truths that should be known and having reached the completion of the final tasks. "Brāhmaṇo bhavaṃ" means from the Avīci hell to the highest plane of existence (bhavagga), there is no Khīṇāsava Brahmin endowed with such birth as the Venerable Gotama; only the Venerable Gotama is truly a Brahmin.

Having said this, the Brahmin filled a golden bowl and offered the milk-rice to the Possessor of Ten Powers. The Teacher, explaining the circumstances and refusing the food, spoke the verse beginning with "Gāthābhigītaṃ me." Therein, "Gāthābhigītaṃ" means that which is sung over with verses. "Abhojaneyyaṃ" means...
213:
It is not fit to be eaten. This is the meaning: Brahmin, for all this time that I have been standing for alms, you were not able to give even a spoonful of food. But now, I have proclaimed all the qualities of the Buddha, as if spreading sesame seeds. This food is like that obtained by singing. Therefore, I should not eat this milk-rice obtained by chanting verses. Brahmin, for those who clearly see the cause and effect, it is not the traditional practice to eat food of this nature. The Buddhas reject food obtained by chanting verses. The Buddhas indeed cast aside food obtained by chanting verses. Brahmin, when the practice of the Noble Ones exists, for those who live depending on the Dhamma and established in the Dhamma, this is the way of life, this is the livelihood. Having rejected food of this nature obtained by singing praises, one should eat only alms-food obtained righteously.

Then the Brahmin thought: "Previously, I did not know whether the recluse Gotama had qualities or not. But now, having known his qualities, a desire has arisen in me to distribute and donate the wealth of about eighty crores in my house to the Dispensation. However, this recluse Gotama says that the requisites given by me are not allowable. The recluse Gotama does not accept my offering." Then the Blessed One, sending forth his omniscience and investigating the Brahmin's thoughts, reflected: "This Brahmin considers all the requisites offered by him to be unallowable. In truth, only that food which was the cause of the conversation is unallowable; the remaining requisites are faultless." Wishing to show the Brahmin the opportunity to donate the four requisites, he spoke the words beginning with "Aññena ca". In those words, "kukkuccha-vūpasantaṃ" means having the hands, body, and speech calmed through the subsiding of restlessness of the hands and so on. "Annena pānena" is merely a teaching method. The meaning is: "Besides this milk-rice which you have marked to give up, serve and offer other requisites such as robes." This means that the Dispensation of the Buddha is like a fertile field that can yield great fruit even from a small seed for you who desire merit. The eighth sutta is finished.

## 9. Sundarikasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, "Sundarika Bhāradvāja" is the name of the Brahmin so called because of his fire sacrifice on the bank of the river named Sundarikā. "Sundarikāya" refers to the river of that name.
214:
Sacrificing to the fire (aggiṃ juhati) means lighting the fire by throwing in offerings such as ghee and sugar. Tending the sacrificial fire (aggihuttaṃ paricarati) means attending to the place of fire sacrifice by sweeping, plastering with cow dung, making offerings, and so on. "Who indeed shall eat this remnant of the offering?" Thinking thus, the Brahmin saw the milk-rice remaining after the fire sacrifice. It is said that the Brahmin thought: "The milk-rice thrown into the fire has been eaten by Mahā Brahmā, but this remnant remains. If I were to give this remnant to a Brahmin born from the mouth of Brahmā, it would please both my father and son, and the path leading to the Brahma world would be well purified." To find a Brahmin, he rose from his seat and looked repeatedly in the four directions, thinking, "Who indeed shall eat this remnant of the offering?"

At the foot of a tree (rukkhamūle) means at the foot of the largest tree in that forest grove. Sitting with his head covered (sasīsaṃ pārutaṃ nisinnaṃ) means sitting with his body and head covered. Why did the Blessed One sit there? It is said that the Blessed One, surveying the world at dawn, saw this Brahmin and thought: "This Brahmin, taking such excellent milk-rice and thinking 'I will feed Mahā Brahmā,' is making it fruitless by burning it in the fire... I shall give him the four paths and the four fruits." Therefore, rising early and attending to his physical needs, he took his bowl and robes and went to sit at the foot of that tree as mentioned.

Then, why did he cover his head? It was to ward off the falling snow and the cold wind. Although the Tathāgata is capable of enduring such cold, if he sat without covering himself, the Brahmin might recognize him from afar and turn back. If that happened, the conversation would not take place. Thus, the Blessed One did this to initiate the conversation, thinking: "When the Brahmin arrives, I will uncover my head. Then, seeing me, what will he say? I will preach the Dhamma according to the course of his words."

He approached (upasaṅkami) means the Brahmin approached with the perception that he was a Brahmin, thinking: "This person is practicing meditation all night with his head covered. I will pour the water of donation for him and give him this remnant of the offering." "This venerable one is shaven-headed; this venerable one is a shaveling"—this was said when the Buddha uncovered his head and the Brahmin saw the short hair-ends, calling him "shaven-headed". Then, looking more closely and not seeing even a topknot, he said "shaveling" out of a desire to disparage. From that very place (tatova) means from the place where he first saw the Blessed One. "There are also those who are shaven-headed" (muṇḍāpi hi) means there are also those who have their heads shaved for some reason.
215:
If you desire the great fruit of giving, do not ask about birth; do not ask about birth. For birth is not the cause of being worthy of offerings. Rather, ask only about conduct (caraṇa) which is distinguished by virtues such as morality (sīla). This conduct alone is the cause of being worthy of offerings. Now, wishing to clarify this meaning, the Buddha said, 'kaṭṭhā have jāyati jātavedo' (fire is indeed born from wood), and so on. The meaning therein is: in this world, fire is born from wood; that fire does not perform the function of fire only when born from pure wood like sal wood, nor does it fail to do so when born from impure wood like a dog’s trough. In fact, because it is endowed with its own qualities such as radiance, it performs the function of fire regardless of the wood from which it is born. In the same way, it is not only one born in a pure family such as a brahmin family who is worthy of offerings, nor is one born in a low family such as a caṇḍāla family unworthy. In fact, whether of low birth or high birth, a monk whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), who is resolute, restrained by shame from evil, and knows what is a cause and what is not, is a noble one (ājānīya). Being thus endowed with qualities such as resolution (dhiti) and shame (hiri), he is a noble recipient of offerings endowed with [true] birth. That khīṇāsava monk maintains wholesome qualities through resolution and restrains unwholesome faults through shame. Furthermore, in this context, 'muni' means one endowed with wisdom; 'dhitimā' means one who possesses steadfast energy; 'ājānīya' means one who knows what is a cause and what is not; 'hirīnisedho' means one who stands having restrained evil through shame. He is tamed by the ultimate truth of the Noble Path. He is endowed with the morality of sense restraint (indriya-saṃvara-sīla). He has reached the end of the four Noble Paths (or he has reached the end of defilements through the Noble Paths). He has lived the holy life of the Noble Path. He possesses the offerings brought near or prepared. Whoever has prepared the offerings should invite that ultimate brahmin. To call out, 'We invite Indra, we invite Soma, we invite Varuṇa, we invite Isāna, we invite Yama,' is useless. When inviting, one should invite that ultimate brahmin only during the mid-day period, saying, 'Venerable sir, it is time; the meal is ready.' Whoever thus invites a khīṇāsava monk at the proper time and establishes the offering of the four requisites there, is said to be sacrificing to a worthy recipient, not by throwing it into an insentient fire.

Thus, hearing the Buddha's words, the brahmin gained confidence and, manifesting his confidence, said 'addhā suyiṭṭhaṃ' and so on. The meaning of those words is: 'Indeed, this offering of mine will now surely be well-given and well-sacrificed; in the past, burning it in the fire was merely useless.' 'Another person' refers to the foolish worldling who says, 'I am a brahmin, I am a brahmin.' The statement 'Please enjoy the remains of the sacrifice' should be understood according to the method already mentioned in the previous sutta. The word 'na cāhaṃ' should be parsed as 'na kho ahaṃ'. Why did the Buddha speak thus? Because as soon as that food was brought near, the deities in the four great islands and the two thousand small islands, thinking 'The Teacher will now eat,' brought flowers, fruits, etc., as well as ghee, butter, oil, honey, molasses, etc., and just as one takes honey by squeezing a honeycomb, they took the nutritive essence (ojā) produced by divine power and infused it. Because of that, the food became extremely subtle. Human bodies are coarse; therefore, because they have coarse bodies, that food cannot be properly digested by humans. Furthermore, because it was cooked by putting sesame seeds in cow's milk, it became food mixed with coarse nutriment. Deities' bodies are subtle; therefore, because they have subtle bodies, that food cannot be properly digested by them. It also cannot be digested in the stomach of a khīṇāsava who is a dry-insight practitioner (sukkhavipassaka). However, a khīṇāsava who has attained the eight attainments could digest it by the power of those attainments. For the Blessed One, he could digest it by his natural karmically-produced heat element (kammaja-tejo).
216:
It refers to the foolish worldling (andhabāla-puthujjana) who says, "I am a brahmin." "Havyasesaṃ" means the food remaining after the sacrifice. The words "Please enjoy, Venerable Sir," and so on, should be understood in the same manner as stated in the previous sutta.

"Na khwāhaṃ" should be parsed as "na kho ahaṃ" (I am certainly not). Why did He speak thus? It is said that as soon as that food was brought near, the deities residing in the four great islands and the two thousand small islands, recognizing that "The Teacher will now eat," brought flowers, fruits, and the like, as well as ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, molasses, and so on. Just as one might squeeze a honeycomb to extract honey, they took only the nutritive essence (ojā) produced by divine power and infused it into the food. Due to this infusion, the food reached a state of extreme subtlety. The physical bodies of humans are coarse; therefore, because they possess coarse bodies, that food does not digest properly for them. Furthermore, because it was cooked by adding sesame seeds to cow's milk, it became food mixed with coarse substance. The physical bodies of deities are subtle; therefore, because they possess subtle bodies, that food does not digest properly for them. It also does not digest in the stomach of a khīṇāsava who is a dry-insight practitioner (sukkhavipassaka). However, a khīṇāsava who has attained the eight meditative attainments (samāpatti) would be able to digest it through the power of those attainments. As for the Blessed One, He could digest it through His natural karmically-produced heat element (kammaja-tejo).

"Appaharite" means in a place where there is no green grass. If it were poured onto green grass, the grass would rot due to the thick, oily milk rice (pāyāsa). The Buddhas do not transgress the training rule regarding the destruction of plants (bhūtagāma-sikkhāpada); therefore, He spoke thus. However, in places where there are large grasses as high as the neck, it is allowable to pour it. "Appāṇake" means that if it were poured into a small amount of water containing living beings, those beings would die; therefore, He spoke thus. In a place where the water is deep and vast, even if a hundred or a thousand bowls of milk rice were poured, the water would not become turbid; it is allowable to pour it into such water. "Opilāpesi" means he caused it to sink along with the golden bowl. "Cicciṭāyati" means it makes a sound like "ciṭiciṭa". If one asks whether this sound was due to the power of the milk rice or the power of the Tathāgata, it was only the power of the Tathāgata. This brahmin, after discarding the milk rice, would have gone away by a side path without coming to the Teacher. At that time, the Blessed One, thinking, "Upon seeing such a marvel, he will come to Me; then, through a Dhamma discourse, I shall break his grip on wrong view, cause him to enter the Dispensation, and let him drink the nectar of the Deathless (Amata)," brought this about through the power of His determination (adhiṭṭhāna).
217:
One who gathers wood is one who burns wood. This burning of wood is external to the Dhamma of the Noble Ones. If purification could be achieved by this burning of wood, then forest fire starters and others who burn much wood would be purified first. 'Kusalā' refers to the wise who are skilled in the aggregates (khandhas) and so forth. 'I kindle the light of wisdom only within myself' means kindling the light of knowledge within one's own continuity (santāna). 'One who has a constant fire' means having a fire that is always blazing with the Omniscient Knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) connected with reflection (āvajjana). 'One who is always concentrated' means having a mind that is always well-established. 'I lead the holy life' refers to the holy life (brahmacariya) practiced at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).

Brahmin, your conceit (māna) is a heavy burden (khāribhāra). For example, just as a four-bushel load carried on the shoulder, though situated above, touches the ground at every step, similarly, conceit raised by depending on the causes of pride such as birth, lineage, and family, causes envy in various places and leads one to sink into the four woeful planes (apāyas). Therefore, He said, 'Brahmin, your conceit is a heavy burden.' 'Anger is the smoke' means anger is called smoke in the sense of defiling your light of knowledge. Your light of knowledge, defiled by that anger, cannot shine. 'Falsehood is the ashes' means falsehood is called ashes in the sense of being lusterless. Just as a fire covered by ashes does not shine, He shows that your knowledge, covered by falsehood, cannot shine. 'The tongue is the sacrificial ladle (sujā)' means just as you have a sacrificial ladle made of gold, silver, copper, iron, wood, or clay, for Me, the extensive tongue is the ladle for the purpose of offering the sacrifice of Dhamma. 'The heart is the fireplace (jotiṭṭhāna)' means just as you have a fireplace on the riverbank, for Me, the hearts of beings are the fireplace in the sense of being the place for offering the sacrifice of Dhamma. 'Attā' refers to the mind (citta).

'Dhamma is the lake (rahada)' means just as you, after serving the fire, with a body defiled by smoke, ashes, and sweat, descend into the Sundarikā River and bathe, for Me, there is no use for an external lake like the Sundarikā River; rather, the Dhamma of the Eightfold Path is My lake. In that lake of the Path, I cause a hundred, a thousand, or eighty-four thousand beings to bathe at once. 'Virtue is the bathing ghat (tittha)' shows that the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhi-sīla) is the landing place for descending into that great lake of Dhamma. 'Unmuddied' (anāvilo) means while your Sundarikā River becomes muddy with sand stirred up from top to bottom even when only four or five people bathe together...
218:
My lake of Dhamma is not like that; even if hundreds of thousands of beings descend and bathe, that lake does not become muddy but remains constantly clear. 'Sabbhi sataṃ pasattho' means the wise are praised by the wise. Or, because of the sublime sense, that person is called 'sa'; being praised by the wise, he is 'sataṃ pasattho'. 'Taranti pāraṃ' means they reach the other shore, which is Nibbāna.

Now, wishing to point out the factors of the lake of the Noble Path, He said 'Saccaṃ dhammo' and so forth. In that context, 'Saccaṃ' is the truth of speech (vacī-sacca). By the word 'dhammo', He shows Right View, Right Thought, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, and Right Concentration. By the word 'saṃyamo', Right Action and Right Livelihood are included. Alternatively, by the word 'saccaṃ', the Path Truth (magga-sacca) is taken. In essence, that Path Truth is Right View. Has it not been said, 'Right View is both the path and the cause'? When Right View is taken, Right Thought is also taken because it follows the same course. By the word 'dhammo', Effort, Mindfulness, and Concentration are taken; by 'saṃyamo', Speech, Action, and Livelihood are taken. In this way, the Eightfold Path is shown. Or else, 'saccaṃ' is the ultimate truth, which in essence is Nibbāna. By the word 'dhammo', the five factors of View, Thought, Effort, Mindfulness, and Concentration are taken. By 'saṃyamo', the three factors of Speech, Action, and Livelihood are taken. In this way too, the Eightfold Path is shown. 'Brahmacariyaṃ' is the holy life that leads to this Nibbāna. 'Majjhe sitā' means being established in the middle (majjhima-paṭipadā), avoiding the two extremes of eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi) and annihilationism (uccheda-diṭṭhi). 'Brahmapatti' means the attainment of the sublime state. In the phrase 'Sa tuju-bhūtesu namo karohi', the letter 'ta' is a euphonic conjunction (padasandhi); the meaning is 'You, pay homage to those who are upright, the Arahants.' 'Tamahaṃ naraṃ dhammasārīti brūmi' means I call such a person who practices thus 'Dhammasārī' (one covered by the garment of Dhamma), or 'one who stands having removed unwholesome states with wholesome states.' The ninth sutta is finished.

## 10. Bahudhītara Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the tenth sutta, 'aññatarasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe' means while the Buddha was surveying the world at dawn, He saw the potential (upanissaya) of that Brahmin to attain Arahantship and thought, 'I will go and assist him,' and thus went to stay in that forest grove. 'Naṭṭhā honti' means the oxen, which were released after plowing and were wandering at the edge of the forest, ran away and were lost while the Brahmin went to eat. 'Pallankaṃ' means sitting with legs crossed (the cross-legged posture). 'Ābhujitvā' means having folded or bent. 'Ujukāyaṃ paṇidhāya' means keeping the upper body erect, connecting the eighteen vertebrae end to end. 'Parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā' means setting up mindfulness directed towards the meditation object, or setting up mindfulness near the mouth (the tip of the nose). Therefore, the Buddha taught in the Vibhaṅga: 'This mindfulness is well-established at the tip of the nose or at the sign of the face; therefore it is said, parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā.' Alternatively, the former method is very appropriate. In another way, the word 'pari' has the sense of grasping/embracing, and the word 'mukhaṃ' has the sense of liberation. Therefore, it is called 'parimukhaṃ satiṃ'. Thus, the meaning of this sutta should also be understood by the method stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga. Embracing the mindfulness that is the cause of liberation from defilements, this is...
219: Sitting cross-legged. "Ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya" means keeping the upper body erect and aligning the eighteen vertebrae end to end. "Parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā" means setting up mindfulness towards the meditation subject, or setting up mindfulness near the mouth (the tip of the nose). For this reason, it is stated in the Vibhaṅga: "This mindfulness is present, well-established at the tip of the nose or at the sign of the mouth; therefore it is said 'setting up mindfulness in front'." Alternatively, according to the method stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: "Pari has the sense of grasping, mukha has the sense of exit (liberation), and sati has the sense of establishment; therefore it is said 'setting up mindfulness in front'." The summary of that method is: "Having established mindfulness as the grasped means of exit (liberation from defilements)." The Blessed One, sitting in this manner, sat emitting the solid six-colored Buddha-rays. "Upasaṅkami" (approached) means that the Brahmin, being oppressed by unhappiness while wandering about, approached thinking, "This ascetic sits so happily indeed." "Ajja saṭṭhiṃ na dissanti" means they have not been seen for six days starting from today. "Pāpakā" means wretched (fruitless) sesame stalks. It is said that on the very day the Brahmin sowed the sesame field, rain fell and caused the sesame seeds to sink into the dust, so they could not produce flowers or fruits. Even those that grew were eaten by pests falling from above, leaving only stalks with one or two leaves. When the Brahmin went to look at the sesame field and saw them, he became unhappy, thinking, "I took these sesames on interest, but now they are destroyed," and based on that, he spoke this verse. "Ussoḷhikāya" means scurrying and jumping about with ears and tails raised with effort. It is said that as his wealth gradually diminished and there was nothing to put in them, his granaries became empty. Then, mice coming from seven houses here and there entered those empty granaries and danced as if playing in a garden; based on that, he spoke thus. "Uppāṭakehi sañchanno" means covered with bedbugs. It is said that there was no one to occasionally clean and tend to the bedding of grass and leaves spread for that Brahmin’s sleep. He would work in the forest during the day and return in the evening to sleep on that bed. Then, the bedbugs would bite him, covering his body all at once; based on that, he spoke thus.
220:
Vidhavā means widows whose husbands have died. As long as there was even a small amount of wealth in that Brahmin’s house, those widows, though they were widows, were allowed to live in their husbands' families' houses. But when he became poor, they were driven out by their parents-in-law and others, saying, "Go to your father’s house," and from there they came to live in that Brahmin’s house. When it was time for the Brahmin to eat, they would send their young children, saying, "Go, eat with your grandfather." When those children lowered their hands into the serving dish, the Brahmin found no space to put his own hand. Based on that, he spoke this verse.

Piṅgalā means one with eyes like those of a tawny cat. Tilakāhatā means one whose body is covered with black and white moles and spots. "Sottaṃ pādena bodheti" means waking someone who has fallen asleep by kicking them with a foot. It is said that this Brahmin, disturbed by the noise of mice and bitten by bedbugs, could not sleep all night and only fell asleep at dawn. Then, just as his eyes were closed, his wife would kick him with her foot to wake him, saying, "Brahmin, what are you doing? The debts you took before and now have reached their peak with interest. Seven daughters must be fed. Now the creditors will come and surround the house; go and work!" Based on that, he spoke this verse.

Iṇāyikā means the creditors from whom this Brahmin had borrowed money. It is said that the Brahmin had borrowed money from many people—one kahāpaṇa from one person, two from another, ten... etc... a hundred from another. Those creditors, not seeing the Brahmin during the day, thought, "We will catch him as soon as he leaves the house," and came to demand payment at the break of dawn. Based on that, he spoke this verse.

When the Brahmin had spoken of his sufferings through these seven verses, the Blessed One, wishing to show, "Brahmin, whatever suffering you have mentioned, I have none of it," increased the Dhamma teaching to the Brahmin with responsive verses. Having heard those verses, the Brahmin gained faith in the Blessed One, established himself in the refuges, ordained, and attained Arahantship. To show this, the words beginning with "Bhāradvājagotto" were spoken. In those words, "alatthā" means "obtained" or "received."

After the Blessed One had ordained that Brahmin, he took him and went to Jetavana. On the following day, taking that Elder as his attendant monk, he went to the gate of King Kosala’s house...
221: (The Blessed One) went (to the door of King Kosala's house). When the King heard that "The Teacher has arrived," he descended from the palace, paid homage, took the bowl from the Teacher's hand, and invited the Blessed One up to the palace. Having seated Him on a noble seat, he washed His feet with scented water, anointed them with oil cooked a hundred times, and had congee brought to be offered. Holding a golden ladle with a silver handle, he offered it to the Teacher. The Teacher closed the bowl (with His hand). The King prostrated at the Blessed One's feet and said, "Venerable Sir, if there is any fault in me, please forgive me." "Great King, there is no fault," He replied. "Then why, Venerable Sir, do you not accept the congee?" he asked. "Great King, there is an impediment (palibodha)," He said. "Venerable Sir, can this impediment be resolved only by not accepting the congee? I am able to resolve this impediment; please accept, Venerable Sir," he pleaded. The Teacher then accepted. The senior monk, having been hungry for a long time, drank as much congee as he desired. The King offered hard and soft food, and at the conclusion of the meal, he paid homage to the Blessed One and said, "Venerable Sir, You were born into the Okkāka dynasty, which has come down through generations; You renounced the glory of a Universal Monarch to go forth and attained the highest state of Buddhahood in the world. Venerable Sir, what kind of impediment do You have?" "Great King, the impediment of this senior monk is just like our own," He replied. The King paid homage to the elder and asked, "Venerable Sir, what kind of impediment do you have?" "Great King, I have the impediment of debt (iṇa)," he replied. "Venerable Sir, how much debt is there?" he asked. "Great King, count it," he said. As the King counted "one, two, a hundred, a thousand," even his fingers were not enough. Then he called a servant and ordered, "Friend, go; let it be proclaimed by drum in the city: 'Let all the creditors of the Brahmin Bahudhītika assemble in the royal courtyard!'" Hearing the sound of the drum, the people assembled. The King had the debt records taken from the hands of those creditors and paid the wealth to all of them without any deficiency. In that payment, the gold alone was worth a hundred thousand. Again, the King asked, "Venerable Sir, is there any other impediment?" "Great King, debt can be escaped by paying it off; but these seven young daughters are great impediments for me," he said. The King sent vehicles, had the elder's daughters brought, treated them as his own daughters, and sent them to their respective family homes. Then he asked again, "Venerable Sir, is there any other impediment?" "Great King, there is still the brahmin lady (wife)," he said. The King sent a vehicle, had the elder's wife brought, placed her in the position of a grandmother, and asked once more, "Venerable Sir, is there any other impediment?"
222:
When he said, "Great King, there is no (impediment)," the King had robes and cloths offered and said, "Venerable Sir, please know that your monkhood is my responsibility." "Very well, Great King," he replied. Then the King said to the elder, "Venerable Sir, all the four requisites such as robes and almsfood will be our responsibility. Venerable Sir, please take the Blessed One's mind to heart and strive in the ascetic's practice." The elder, as the King had requested, practiced the ascetic's Dhamma without negligence and before long reached the destruction of the taints, the fruit of Arahantship. The tenth sutta is finished.

## Pahamovaggo (The First Chapter).

## 2. Upāsakavagga (The Chapter on Lay Followers)

## 1. Kasibhāradvāja Sutta Vaṇṇanā (Commentary on the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta)

In the first sutta of the second chapter, "Magadhesu" means in the country named Magadha. "Dakkhiṇāgirismiṃ" means there is a district to the south of the mountain that surrounds the city of Rājagaha; the monastery in that district also has the same name. "Ekanāḷāyaṃ brāhmaṇagāme" means Ekanāḷā is the name of that village. Many brahmins live in that village, or it is a village whose revenue is enjoyed by brahmins. Therefore, it is called "Brāhmaṇagāmo" (Brahmin village).

"Tena kho pana samayena" (At that time) means at the time when the Blessed One was dwelling in the Great Monastery of Dakkhināgiri, depending on the brahmin village of Ekanāḷā in the country of Magadha, awaiting the maturation of the brahmin's spiritual faculties. "Kasibhāradvājassa" means that brahmin lived depending on farming (kasi); Bhāradvāja was his clan name. "Pañcamattāni" means five hundred in measure, meaning exactly five hundred ploughs, neither more nor less. "Payuttāni" means harnessed, meaning they were attached with yokes and straps placed on the shoulders of the oxen.

"Vappakāle" means at the time of sowing, the season for scattering seeds. In that context, there are two types of sowing: sowing in mud (kalalavappa) and sowing in dust (paṃsuvappa). Here, sowing in dust is intended, and that too is the auspicious sowing (maṅgalavappa) performed on the first day. The completeness of the equipment at that auspicious time was as follows: three thousand great oxen were stationed nearby; all those oxen had their horns covered with gold and had hooves made of silver...
223:
All the oxen were decorated with white garlands and five-finger marks of scented paste. They were perfect in their five limbs and possessed all auspicious characteristics. Some oxen were as black as collyrium, some as white as crystal, some as red as coral, and some were variegated like masāragalla stone.

In this manner, five hundred plowmen, dressed in brand new white garments and decorated with scents and garlands, placed flower wreaths on their right shoulders. Their bodies were radiant and bright, anointed with yellow orpiment, red arsenic, and collyrium. They proceeded in groups, with ten plows in each group. The tips of the plows, the yokes, and the goads were inlaid with gold. Eight large oxen were yoked to the first main plow, while four were yoked to each of the remaining plows. The rest of the oxen were brought along to be rotated with those that became weary. In each group, one person would plow while another followed, sowing seeds from a seed-cart.

The Brahmin, having previously had his beard trimmed, bathed, and anointed himself with highly fragrant scents, dressed in a cloth worth five hundred and draped an upper robe worth a thousand over one shoulder. He wore twenty rings, two on each finger, lion-shaped earrings in his ears, and a turban like a Brahma-crown on his head. Adorned with a golden garland around his neck and surrounded by a company of Brahmins, he directed and managed the work. Then, the Brahmin's wife had milk-rice cooked in countless pots, loaded them onto large carts, bathed in scented water, and, adorned with all kinds of ornaments and surrounded by a company of women, went to the workplace. The Brahmin's house was also smeared with green cow dung, scattered with parched rice, and decorated with full water pots, banana trees, and banners. Ritual offerings to the deities were well-prepared with scents, flowers, and other items. In the fields, banners and flags were hoisted in various places. The gathering, including attendants and workers, numbered about two thousand five hundred. All were dressed in brand new garments. Milk-rice was prepared as the sole food for everyone.

Then the Brahmin had a golden bowl washed, filled it with milk-rice, and prepared it with ghee, honey, and molasses, then performed the ritual offering for the plows. The Brahmin's wife had bowls made of gold, silver, bronze, copper, and iron distributed to the five hundred plowmen, and taking a golden ladle, she went about serving them with milk-rice. The Brahmin, having completed the ritual offerings, put on sandals with red straps, and holding a staff with a red-gold handle, wandered about directing: "Pour milk-rice here, pour sugar here..."
224:
"...pour ghee here, pour sugar in this bowl," he wandered about giving instructions. This was the manner in which the work proceeded.

In the monastery, wherever the Buddhas reside, they have five daily duties. These are: the pre-meal duty (purebhattakicca), the post-meal duty (pacchābhattakicca), the first-watch duty (purimayāmakicca), the middle-watch duty (majjhimayāmakicca), and the last-watch duty (pacchimayāmakicca).

Among these five duties, this is the pre-meal duty: The Buddha rises early in the morning and, for the benefit of his attendants and for his own physical comfort, performs preparatory acts such as washing his face. Until the time for alms-round, he spends his time in a secluded seat in the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti). When it is time for alms-round, he adjusts his inner robe, fastens his waistband, puts on his upper robe, and takes his bowl. Sometimes alone, sometimes surrounded by the Sangha of monks, he enters a village or a market town for alms. Sometimes he enters in his natural form, and sometimes accompanied by many miraculous wonders.

These are the wonders: As the Lord of the World enters for alms, gentle winds precede him and cleanse the ground. Clouds sprinkle drops of water to settle the dust on the path and then remain above as a canopy. Other winds bring flowers and scatter them on the path. High places on the ground level out, and low places rise up. When he sets down his feet, the ground becomes perfectly even, or else soft-to-the-touch lotus flowers receive his feet. As soon as he places his right foot inside the threshold, six-colored rays emit from his body, running here and there, making palaces and pinnacled gables appear as if sprinkled with liquid gold or draped with variegated cloth. Elephants, horses, birds, and other animals, remaining in their respective places, make sweet sounds. Likewise, musical instruments such as drums and lutes, and even the ornaments worn by people, produce melodious sounds.

By these signs, people know, "Today the Blessed One has entered here for alms." Dressed and robed properly, they take scents, flowers, and other offerings, leave their houses, reach the street, and respectfully worship the Blessed One with scents and flowers. They request, "Venerable Sir, give us ten monks," "Give us twenty," or "Give us a hundred monks," and taking the Buddha's bowl, they prepare seats and respectfully serve them with alms-food.
225:
After the Blessed One had finished his meal, he surveyed the mental dispositions of the people and taught the Dhamma in such a way that some were established in the Three Refuges, some in the Five Precepts, some in one of the fruits of Stream-entry, Once-returning, or Non-returning, and some, having gone forth, were established in the supreme fruit of Arahantship. Having thus benefited the multitude, he rose from his seat and went to the monastery. There, he sat on the noble Buddha-seat prepared in the perfumed pavilion, waiting for the monks to finish their meal. Then, when the monks' meal was finished, the attendant monk informed the Blessed One. Thereupon, the Blessed One entered the Gandhakuṭi. This is the pre-meal duty (purebhattakicca).

Then, the Blessed One, having performed the pre-meal duties, sat in the attendance hall of the Gandhakuṭi, washed his feet, and standing on the footstool, exhorted the assembly of monks: "Monks, strive with diligence; the arising of a Buddha in the world is rare, the attainment of human birth is rare, the perfection of faith is rare, going forth is rare, and hearing the True Dhamma is rare." Then, some monks asked the Blessed One for meditation subjects. The Blessed One gave them meditation subjects suitable for their temperaments. Then, all the monks, having paid homage to the Blessed One, went to their respective places for the night and day. Some went to the forest, some to the foot of a tree, some to a mountain or similar place, some to the realm of the Four Great Kings... and some to the realm of the Vasavatti devas. Then, the Blessed One entered the Gandhakuṭi and, if he so desired, mindfully and clearly comprehending, he would lie down for a moment in the lion's posture on his right side. Then, with his body refreshed, he rose and, in the second part of the afternoon, surveyed the world of beings to be guided. In the third part, he would stay depending on a village or market town; there, the people, having given alms before the meal, would gather at the monastery after the meal, well-dressed and well-robed, bringing perfumes, flowers, and so on. Then, the Blessed One, proceeding with suitable psychic power to the assembled company, sat on the noble Buddha-seat prepared in the Dhamma hall and taught the Dhamma appropriate to the time and occasion. Then, knowing the time, he dismissed the assembly, and the people, having paid homage to the Blessed One, departed. This is the post-meal duty (pacchābhattakicca).

Having thus completed the post-meal duties, if he wished to bathe his body, he rose from the Buddha-seat, entered the bathroom, and refreshed his body with water prepared by the attendant monk. The attendant monk also brought the Buddha-seat, dusted it, and spread it in the courtyard of the Gandhakuṭi. The Blessed One, having put on his well-dyed lower robe, fastened his waistband, and properly adjusted his upper robe, came there and...
226:
He sat alone for a moment in the seclusion of fruition attainment (phalasamāpatti). Then, monks came from various places to attend upon the Blessed One. There, some asked questions, some asked for meditation subjects, and some requested to hear the Dhamma. The Blessed One, fulfilling their desires, spent the first watch of the night. This is the duty of the first watch (purimayāmakicca).

At the conclusion of the first watch, when the monks had paid homage to the Blessed One and departed, the deities of the entire ten thousand world systems, obtaining the opportunity, approached the Blessed One and asked questions as they had prepared them, even those as short as four syllables. The Blessed One, answering the questions of those various deities, spent the middle watch of the night. This is the duty of the middle watch (majjhimayāmakicca).

The last watch of the night, however, he divided into three parts. To relieve the fatigue of the body caused by sitting since before the meal, he spent one part in walking meditation. In the second part, he entered the Gandhakuṭi and, mindfully and clearly comprehending, lay down in the lion's posture on his right side. In the third part, he rose and sat down, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye (buddhacakkhu) to see those individuals who had performed meritorious deeds such as giving and virtue in the presence of former Buddhas. This is the duty of the last watch (pacchimayāmakicca).

At that time, while thus surveying, he saw the Brahmin Kasibhāradvāja, who was endowed with the supporting conditions for Arahantship. He thought: "When I go there, a conversation will take place. At the end of the conversation, having heard the Dhamma teaching, this Brahmin, along with his wife and children, will be established in the Three Refuges. Having distributed eighty crores of wealth in my dispensation, he will later renounce the world, go forth, and attain Arahantship." Knowing this, he went there, initiated a conversation, and taught the Dhamma. To show this matter, the words beginning with "Atha kho Bhagavā" were spoken.

In that Pali text, "pubbaṇhasamayaṃ" is the second case (accusative) used in the sense of the seventh case (locative), meaning "in the morning." "Nivāsetvā" means having dressed. This is said in the sense of changing into the monastery robe. "Pattacīvaramādāya" means taking the bowl with the hands and the robe with the body, receiving and carrying them. It is heard that, as the Blessed One desired to enter for alms, the stone bowl, having the color of an emerald (indranīla), came into the middle of his two hands like a bee coming into the middle of two blooming lotuses. Having received the bowl that came thus with his hands, and carrying the robe that was wrapped around him evenly with his body, is what is meant.
227:
'Te nupasaṅkami' means that the Blessed One approached alone by the very path that one must take to reach the plowing festival. Why did the monks not follow the Blessed One? Whenever the Blessed One wished to go somewhere alone, he would close the door and stay inside the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi) until the time for the alms-round. By that sign, the monks knew, "Today the Blessed One wishes to wander for alms alone; he has surely seen someone who is fit to be tamed." Those monks would then take their own bowls and robes, circumambulate the Fragrant Chamber, pay their respects, and go on their alms-round. On that occasion, too, the Blessed One acted in this manner, which is why the monks did not follow him.

'Parivesanā vattati' means that the task of serving the five hundred plowmen, who sat holding golden vessels and so forth, was not yet finished. 'Ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi' means he stood in a high place where the Brahmin could see him, where it was easy to hear his words, and within sight. While standing there, he emitted a bodily radiance from all directions, yellow like liquid silver and gold, surpassing the brilliance of the moon and the sun. Due to the pervading influence of that radiance, the walls of the Brahmin's workshop, the trees, and the clods of earth turned up by the plow appeared as if they were made of gold. Then the people, whether eating or plowing, abandoned all their tasks. They saw the Fully Enlightened One standing in a suitable place, his body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (Mahāpurisalakkhaṇa) and accompanied by the eighty minor characteristics (Asīti-anubyañjana), beautified by a fathom-wide aura, with a pair of arms like a moving lotus pond, like the sky filled with a host of stars shining with nets of rays, and like a golden mountain peak entwined with lightning, blazing with glory. They washed their hands and feet, raised their joined palms in salutation, and stood surrounding the Blessed One. Seeing the Blessed One standing for alms while surrounded by the crowd, the Brahmin Kasibhāradvāja said to the Blessed One, "O ascetic, I plow and I sow."

Why did the Brahmin say this? Was it because he lacked faith in the Tathāgata, who is inspiring in every direction and has attained supreme self-control and tranquility? Or was it out of stinginess regarding a single spoonful of alms-food, even though he had prepared milk-rice for two thousand five hundred people? It was not for either of those reasons. Rather, seeing his people abandon their work because they were not satisfied with gazing at the Blessed One, he felt displeased, thinking, "He has come to ruin my work."

Furthermore, seeing the perfection of the Blessed One's marks, he thought, "If this person were to engage in work, he would be like a crest-gem on the heads of the people in the whole of Jambudīpa. Why should his welfare not be fulfilled? Why does he, out of laziness, not work and instead wander for alms at festivals such as this plowing ceremony?" Thus he was displeased. Therefore, he said, "O ascetic, I plow and I sow; only after plowing and sowing do I eat."
228:
Therefore, he spoke thus. Seeing the perfection of the Blessed One's marks, he thought: "If this person were to manage affairs and work, he would be like a crest-gem on the heads of the people in the whole of Jambudīpa. Why should his prosperity not be complete? In this way, due to laziness, he does not manage affairs but wanders for alms at plowing festivals and the like." Thus, the Brahmin was displeased. Therefore, he said: "O ascetic, I plow and I sow; having plowed and sown, I eat."

This was his intention: "My works are not ruined; I am still striving. I am not endowed with marks like you. You, too, should plow and sow and eat. For one endowed with such marks as you, what prosperity would not be fulfilled?" Alternatively, he had heard: "A prince was born in the Sakyan royal family; he renounced the sovereignty of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) and went forth." Knowing now that "This is he," and wishing to reproach him, he said: "Having renounced the sovereignty of a Universal Monarch, you are now exhausted." There is yet another view: this Brahmin was one of sharp wisdom. He did not speak because he lacked faith in the Blessed One. Rather, seeing the perfection of the Blessed One's physical form and honoring the perfection of his merit, he spoke thus to initiate a conversation. Then the Blessed One, according to the disposition of the one to be tamed, showed his own status as the supreme plowman and sower in the world with its devas, saying: "O Brahmin, I too..." and so on.

Then the Brahmin thought: "This ascetic says, 'I too plow and sow.' Yet I do not see his coarse plowing implements such as the yoke and plow. How is this? Does he speak a falsehood?" Examining the Blessed One from the soles of his feet to the tips of his hair using the science of body marks (Aṅgavijjā), and knowing that he was endowed with the thirty-two excellent marks of a Great Man because of his performed merits, he thought: "It is impossible for such a person to speak a falsehood." With great respect arising, he abandoned the address 'ascetic' (Samana) and addressed the Blessed One by his clan name, saying: "We do not see the Venerable Gotama's..." and so on. Because it is the power of the Buddhas to speak in accordance with the Dhamma previously established, the Blessed One, demonstrating the Buddha-power, said: "Faith is the seed," and so on.

What is this "accordance with the Dhamma previously established"? Did the Brahmin not ask the Blessed One about the connection with plowing implements like the plow? Yet the Blessed One spoke of the seed, which was not asked about, as being of a similar nature: "Faith is the seed." If this is so, the speech would also be disconnected and inconsistent in its sequence (Anusandhi). For the Buddhas...
229:
In the speech of the Buddhas, there is no such thing as disconnected discourse, nor do they teach in a manner that is inconsistent with the Dhamma previously taken up. In this teaching, the connection of sequence (anusandhi) should be understood as follows: The Brahmin asked the Blessed One about farming by way of the components of farming such as the yoke and the plow. Out of compassion for that Brahmin, the Blessed One, not omitting even the unasked matters, wished to make known the nature of farming together with its root, its support, its components, and its fruit. Thus, showing it starting from the very foundation, He said: "Faith is the seed," and so forth.

In that statement, the seed is the foundation of farming. This is because farming is performed only when there is seed, and not when there is no seed; and it is performed according to the measure of the seed. Skilled farmers plow the field in accordance with the amount of seed, thinking, "Let our crops not diminish," and they do not plow in excess, thinking, "Let our effort not be in vain." Since the seed alone is the foundation, the Blessed One, showing the components of farming starting from the foundation, and wishing to show the Dhamma first taken up in His own farming which is consistent with the seed first taken up in that Brahmin's farming, said: "Faith is the seed." In this way, the consistency of the Dhamma first taken up should also be understood.

If it is asked, "Why were the unasked matters not spoken after first stating only what was asked?" it is because such a teaching is beneficial and is capable of connecting with the benefit of the Dhamma. Indeed, this Brahmin was wise, but having been born in a family of wrong view, he was devoid of faith. A wise person who is devoid of faith cannot practice in a matter that is not his own domain through the faith of others, and thus cannot attain distinction. Furthermore, his weak faith, being overwhelmed by the defilement of impurity, even if it exists alongside powerful wisdom, cannot accomplish the goal, just like an ox yoked to the same shaft as an elephant. Thus, faith is beneficial to him. Wishing to establish that Brahmin in faith, this meaning which should have been spoken later was spoken first due to skillfulness in teaching. Moreover, rain is beneficial to the seed; stating the matter of rain immediately after that [seed] is capable of connecting it with the benefit. Thus, because of the ability to connect the Dhamma, this meaning which should have been spoken later, as well as other meanings such as the plow-pole and the bond, should be understood as having been spoken first.

In that teaching, faith has the characteristic of clarity (sampasāda) or the characteristic of conviction (okappana). "Seed" (bīja) refers to five kinds of seeds: root-seed, stem-seed, joint-seed, bud-seed, and seed-seed as the fifth. All of these are designated as "seed" in the sense of germinating and growing.
230:
In that teaching of "Faith is the seed" and so forth, by way of analogy, the seed which is the cause in the Brahmin's farming performs two functions: it stands firmly below by the root and it causes the sprout to rise above. Similarly, faith, which is the cause in the Blessed One's farming, stands firmly below by the root of virtue (sīla) and causes the sprout of tranquility and insight (samatha-vipassanā) to rise above. Furthermore, just as that grain seed, taking the essence of earth and the essence of water through the root, grows through the stalk to receive the ripening of the grain, so this faith, taking the essence of tranquility and insight meditation through the root of virtue, grows through the stalk of the Noble Path (ariya-magga) to obtain the ripening of the grain of the Noble Fruit (ariya-phala).

Just as that grain seed, being established in good soil, reaches growth, increase, and abundance through the development of roots, sprouts, leaves, stalks, and stems, and producing milk, accomplishes the rice-ear filled with countless grains; so this faith, being established in the mental continuum, reaches growth, increase, and abundance through the six purifications (visuddhi), and producing the milk of the purification of knowledge and vision (ñāṇadassana-visuddhi), accomplishes the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala) filled with many analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) and direct knowledges (abhiññā). Therefore, He said: "Faith is the seed."

But why is only faith called the "seed" when more than fifty other wholesome states arise together with it? It is because it performs the function of a seed. Just as among those states, consciousness (viññāṇa) alone performs the function of cognizing, so faith performs the function of a seed. And it is the foundation of all wholesome states. As it is said: "One who has faith approaches; approaching, he attends... and through wisdom, he fully penetrates and sees that Dhamma."

It is called "tapa" (ardor/austerity) because it causes unwholesome states and the body to burn. This is a designation for sense restraint (indriya-saṃvara), energy (vīriya), ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), and difficult practices (dukkara-kārikā); however, in this context, sense restraint is intended. "Vuṭṭhi" (rain) is of many kinds, such as rainfall and wind-rain, but here rainfall is intended. Just as the seed and the crops caused by the seed, being well-supported by the Brahmin's rainfall, grow and reach completion without withering; so the faith and the states such as virtue rooted in faith, being well-supported by the Blessed One's sense restraint, grow and reach completion without withering. Therefore, He said: "Ardor is the rain."

In the phrase "paññā me" (my wisdom), the word "me" should also be applied to the preceding terms as "my faith is the seed, my ardor is the rain." What is shown by this? It should be understood thus: "Brahmin, in the field sown by you, if there is rain, it is well. If there is no rain, water must be brought from rivers, lakes, or dams. Similarly, when I have yoked the oxen of energy, having bound them together with the bond of the mind to the plow-pole of shame (hiri) and the yoke and plow of wisdom, and having prodded them with the goad of mindfulness, there is no such thing as a lack of rain when the seed of faith is sown in the field of my own mental continuum. Indeed, for me, this state of sense restraint is always like the rain of ardor."

Although wisdom (paññā) is of many kinds, such as that of the sense sphere, in this context, the Path-wisdom (magga-paññā) together with tranquility and insight is intended. "Yuganangalaṃ" means the yoke and the plow. Brahmin, just as you yoke the yoke and the plow, the twofold wisdom of the Blessed One is the yoke and the plow. In that statement, just as the yoke is the support for the plow-pole and is bound to the plow-pole at the front, and being the support for the bonds, it restrains the oxen by knowing their movement so they go straight without swerving to one side; so wisdom is the support for states such as shame. Therefore, it is said: "All wholesome states have wisdom as their chief," and "Among wholesome states, wisdom is said to be the best."
231:
Once (the seed of faith) is sown, there is no such thing as a lack of rain; indeed, for me, this practice of sense-restraint (indriya-saṃvara-tapa) is always like rain.

Although wisdom (paññā) is of many kinds, such as those belonging to the sense sphere and so on, in this context, it refers to Path-wisdom (magga-paññā) together with insight (vipassanā). 'Yuganangala' refers to the yoke and the plow. Just as a Brahmin has a yoke and a plow, the Blessed One also has both insight and wisdom. In that context, just as the yoke is the support for the shaft (īsā), is tied to the shaft in front, is the support for the ropes (yotta), and maintains the oxen moving together, so too wisdom is the supporting condition (upanissaya) for states such as shame (hirī).

Therefore, it was said: "All wholesome states have wisdom as their chief," and "The wise say wisdom is best among wholesome states, like the moon among stars." Wisdom stands in front because it precedes wholesome states. As it is said: "Virtue, glory, and the Dhamma of the virtuous follow one who possesses wisdom." Because it arises without being separated from shame, it is like being tied to the shaft. Because it is the supporting condition for the rope of concentration (samādhi) known as 'mind' (mano), it is the support for the ropes. By preventing over-exertion and laxity, it maintains the oxen of energy (vīriya) moving together.
